analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal drinking-water rules on lead: more testing, public reporting, and full lead pipe replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill to strengthen federal lead-in-water rules after the lead and copper rule was referred to a House subcommittee in April 2017 and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the EPA to rewrite the federal Lead and Copper Rule so that water systems test more often and more honestly, report results publicly, tell residents within 2 days when lead is found above the action level, map and publish the location of lead service lines, and replace entire lead pipes instead of cutting them in half. It also would have forced the allowable lead level down from 15 parts per billion to 10 by the end of 2020 and 5 by the end of 2026. It never moved past its first referral to a subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents served by public water systems, especially children, pregnant women, and renters in older homes with lead service lines, who would get faster notice of lead findings, on-site investigations of contaminated taps, public maps of lead pipes, and a tighter health standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families drinking from lead service lines

how_it_helps.text: Requires public water systems to notify people at a specific facility within 2 days of detecting lead above the action level, and to complete an on-site investigation to find the lead source within 10 business days [S2] [S3].

Bans water-system sampling techniques that minimize the detection of lead, requires at least annual sampling, prioritizes testing at high-risk buildings, and requires sampling at all drinking-water taps in schools and child care centers [S3].

Requires water systems to build and publish, within 3 years, an inventory and online map of the material composition of every service line, plus the legal documents establishing who owns those lines [S2] [S3].
Requires systems to replace an entire lead service line, instead of the partial replacements that can temporarily raise lead levels, whenever replacement occurs [S2].

Requires EPA to lower the lead action level in drinking water to no more than 10 parts per billion by December 31, 2020, and no more than 5 parts per billion by December 31, 2026, down from the 15 parts per billion standard then in effect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities and the communities they serve, through the cost of more frequent and more honest sampling, building line inventories, conducting on-site investigations, and replacing full lead service lines; some of that cost could reach water ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls heavily on water utilities, and these costs are typically recovered through water rates, so households would pay some of the price of testing, inventories, and full lead line replacement [S3].

Replacing every lead service line is expensive, and where the utility owns only part of the line, the bill's public education materials contemplate financial assistance to line owners, but the bill does not itself fund the work [S3].

Tightening the action level from 15 to 10 and then 5 parts per billion would classify many more systems as in violation, triggering mandatory public notification and treatment changes that impose real costs even where individual health risk is debated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large and well documented: no safe level of lead exposure exists for children, and the bill targeted the exact transparency failures that let lead contamination go undetected. The costs are real but ordinary for a public-health standard, and were the kind of expense water systems had already been deferring for decades. The bill's main design weakness is that it imposed mandates without dedicated funding, which would have shifted some costs to ratepayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment subcommittee in April 2017, and no hearing, markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Kildee introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, with 8 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 6, 2017, and to the Subcommittee on Environment on April 7, 2017 [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: it never received a subcommittee or committee vote, was never reported out of committee, and never reached the House floor [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died on the calendar without a vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water utilities came out ahead: they avoided any new obligation to sample honestly, disclose lead findings within days, map their lead lines, or replace lead service lines in full. Residents of older homes continued living with the pre-2017 rules and the 15 parts-per-billion standard.

for.name: Rep. Dan Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, to tighten federal lead-in-water rules on testing, disclosure, and lead service line replacement.

for.name: 8 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all eight were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action: no hearing, no markup, no vote to send it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 7, 2017, and held no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on or advanced the bill in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities to sample more rigorously, publish lead line maps, investigate contaminated taps within days, and replace lead service lines in full, all at their expense. Under existing rules, utilities could report fewer or partial results and replace lines partially, and no such bill ever reached a vote.

A mandate to fully inventory and replace lead service lines nationwide would have created major replacement work. Because the bill died, that work stayed limited to what utilities and cities chose to do on their own.
